syllabus.clause: why knapsack has an O(nW) DP while bin packing has no pseudo-polynomial algorithm unless P = NP

at.step: That table's size is the item count times the capacity itself, not times the length of the capacity written down. Ten bits of capacity gives about a hundred thousand cells; twenty bits gives about a hundred million; forty bits gives over a hundred trillion, for the same hundred items.

Bin packing's own hardness depends on the interaction of many bins with many different sizes. Fix the number of bins and it becomes pseudo-polynomial in the capacity; fix the bin capacity instead and it becomes polynomial outright. Neither fix is available when both are free to vary.

Write that same capacity as a short string of bits, or as one tally mark for every unit of value. The table's size tracks the tally strip's length, not the bit string's. That table is pseudo-polynomial: polynomial in the number itself, exponential in how compactly it is written.

A problem is strongly NP-hard when it remains NP-hard even with every numerical parameter bounded by a polynomial in the input's length — the same thing as staying hard when every number is written in unary. Three-partition is the standard example of exactly this.

items.item: the strong NP-completeness definition: NP-complete even when every numerical parameter is bounded by a polynomial in the input's length

at.step: A problem is strongly NP-hard when it remains NP-hard even with every numerical parameter bounded by a polynomial in the input's length — the same thing as staying hard when every number is written in unary. Three-partition is the standard example of exactly this.

items.item: bin packing is strongly NP-complete while 0-1 knapsack is only weakly NP-complete

at.step: Suppose a strongly NP-hard problem did have a pseudo-polynomial algorithm. Bounding its numbers by a polynomial would then make that algorithm run in ordinary polynomial time — but the problem is, by definition, still NP-hard on exactly those bounded instances. That is the contradiction.

items.item: a weakly NP-hard problem may have a pseudo-polynomial algorithm; partition is an example

at.step: A problem is weakly NP-hard when it is hard only in the usual, compact binary encoding, and a pseudo-polynomial algorithm may still exist for it, the way it does for knapsack. The partition problem is the standard example: shrink its numbers and the hard instances disappear.

items.item: a strongly NP-hard problem has no pseudo-polynomial algorithm and no fully polynomial-time approximation scheme

at.step: Strong NP-hardness rules out more than an exact algorithm: a strongly NP-hard problem with a polynomially bounded objective also has no fully polynomial-time approximation scheme, unless P equals NP. Knapsack's own such scheme, built on its weak hardness, belongs to a later topic on approximation.

items.item: the decision form of knapsack is NP-complete

at.step: The decision form of knapsack — can a value of at least some target be reached without exceeding the weight limit — is NP-complete. And yet a dynamic program with one row per item and one column per unit of capacity fills in and answers it in a single pass.

items.item: knapsack has a pseudo-polynomial time algorithm using dynamic programming, and that runtime is not polynomial in the input's length, which is why it does not contradict NP-completeness

at.step: A knapsack with a hundred items and a capacity measured in bits fills a table in a blink: about a hundred thousand cells. Append ten more bits to that capacity and the table has about a hundred million. Append thirty more and it is over a hundred trillion, though the input itself grew by only thirty bits.

items.item: bin packing is strongly NP-complete, proven by reducing the strongly NP-complete 3-partition problem to it

at.step: Bin packing is also NP-complete, and it also has numbers in it. Does shrinking those numbers give it the same kind of escape that knapsack's table gives knapsack?

items.item: bin packing is solvable in pseudo-polynomial time for any fixed number of bins K, and in polynomial time for any fixed bin capacity B

items.item: 3-partition is strongly NP-complete: deciding whether a multiset of integers can be partitioned into equal-sum triplets

at.step: A backtracking solver on three-partition instances with every number kept small still fans out sharply as more triples are added: the search tree's size climbs fast even though no single number in the instance ever grows.

items.item: 3-partition remains NP-complete even when its integers are bounded by a polynomial in n, the same as being hard in unary

at.step: Three-partition's hard instances keep every number small by design: the numbers are bounded by a polynomial in how many of them there are. Does that smallness buy the same escape it bought partition, or is something different going on here?
